# 5 Nano Banana Workflows: One Upload, a Whole Set of Images Out

> **In short:** Nano Banana — the nickname for Google's image model — runs "workflows" that take one uploaded image and return a whole set of variations in a single step, so a logo, portrait, or product photo becomes a complete toolkit rather than a single file.

A few months ago, getting a usable set of images from one source meant hours of manual editing. You'd shoot once, then resize for different platforms, swap backgrounds, and tweak lighting one file at a time. New AI image tools can now chain those steps together. Feed in one file, and a finished set comes back.

## What a "workflow" actually means

In plain terms, a workflow is a recipe. You give the tool a starting image — say, a logo — and tell it what you want at the end: a social media banner, a business card version, a phone wallpaper. The tool handles each step (resizing, recoloring, reframing) without you clicking between them.

Nano Banana made waves for doing this in one shot. You describe what you want, and the tool plans the steps itself. That's the difference between an image generator (one prompt, one image) and a workflow (one prompt, a connected set of outputs).

## Five practical uses people are trying

These examples work for both personal projects and small business work. None of them need a design background.

**1. Logo to a full brand kit.** Upload your logo once, and the tool produces a dark-mode version, a single-color stamp, a square social media avatar, and a horizontal banner. Useful when you're starting a side project and don't want to pay a designer yet.

**2. Portrait to a set of headshots.** One casual photo becomes several formal-looking versions with different backgrounds and lighting — handy for LinkedIn, a company directory, or a conference badge.

**3. One product photo to a small catalog.** Upload a single product image (a coffee mug, a candle, a chair), and the workflow returns a white-background listing version, a styled lifestyle shot, and a close-up detail view. Helpful if you sell on a marketplace and don't have a photo studio.

**4. Street photo to seasonal variations.** A photo of a building or park becomes the same scene in autumn colors, in snow, at golden hour, and at night. Useful for travel blogs, real estate listings, or just experimenting.

**5. Room photo to staged interiors.** A photo of an empty or messy room turns into a few furnished versions in different styles. Helpful when you're planning a redecoration and want to preview options.

## What this means for you

- **If you run a small business or side project:** these workflows replace several hours of fiddling in design software. You won't get pixel-perfect results every time, but you get a starting set in minutes and can adjust from there.
- **If you just want better personal photos:** a workflow can give you a few options from one upload, so you don't have to reshoot every time you want a different look.
- **If you're new to AI image tools:** start with one workflow. The logo-to-brand-kit example is the simplest to test, because the input is small and the results are easy to judge.
- **A practical caution:** the output still needs a human look. AI-generated sets often have small errors — a wrong letter on a logo, an extra finger in a portrait, an off-color wall. Always check before you publish.

## Wrap-up

The shift worth noticing is small but real: one good source image is no longer the end of a project. With the right workflow, it's the beginning of a whole set. Pick one workflow this week that matches something you actually need — a logo, a product, a room — and see what comes back.
